The instructor’s strongest point is that she clearly has strong academic knowledge of the subject and high expectations for students’ work. She was also generally a nice and respectful person in her interactions with students. However, in my experience, the organization and consistency of the course created several difficulties. One of these issues was the grading standard. It was stated after an exam that only “publishable work” would receive full points on exams and essays, which felt like an unrealistic and unclear expectation for an undergraduate course. This made the grading scale feel somewhat discouraging and difficult to understand. Another concern was the last-minute cancellation of classes, which happened on two or three occasions. For example, one class was cancelled only around 30 to 40 minutes before it was supposed to begin, with a very brief email such as “I have to cancel class, sorry”. This was an especially difficult situation for students who lived far from campus and needed to wake up one or two hours earlier in order to attend these lectures. For this reason, these cancellations felt rather unprofessional and inconsiderate of students’ time. Attendance was also handled inconsistently. Attendance was not taken during the first few weeks of the semester, then it was taken for several weeks, and then it stopped again. This made the attendance policy unclear and unevenly applied. Overall, while I think the instructor was respectful and knowledgeable, the course suffered from issues related to organization, consistency, grading expectations, attendance policy, and communication. These factors contributed to the feeling that the course was not conducted with the level of professionalism expected from an instructor, particularly one in a senior academic role.

In an email that was sent by our professor stated that “The class is too small for me to be able to assign an A+ “ and another email; “I cannot assign an A+ in a class this size (nobody would produce publishable work in an exam anyway). So the highest possible grade is in the straight A range, 90-95… a student who gets a 91 should not worry about not getting a 97, because that is not possible”. This policy made it feel like grades were decided in advance, and no one could achieve the highest possible grade no matter how well they performed.

The quiz policy about bringing the book, Harvest was also unfair. In a class email, she wrote  “50 pts for bringing a copy of the novel… and 50 pt for answering a basic reading comprehension question.” This was announced only about 46 hours before the class. Within that short amount of time, we were expected to purchase the book, read the assigned chapter, and come to class prepared for a graded quiz. Her decision felt too rushed. Not all students (like me) can immediately afford a required book in such a short time, and this made it feel like grades depended on access and money, rather than effort.

The way class cancellations were handled was also frustrating. For example, one email said, “No class today… Two hrs on Thurs, pls,” and this was sent shortly before class time. Not all students live close to campus, and some of us have to wake up early to come class. Thus, it created unnecessary inconvenience.

The communication style in emails also felt unprofessional (e.g, the previous email quote). The use of informal language like “pls” or “AI slop,” as well as statements like “nobody would produce publishable work in an exam anyway,” did not sound appropriate for a university course, especially when the professor expects academic and professional standards from the students.
